name: The Ruxton Liberty Tree

location.address: Intersection of Dunlora Road and Bellona Avenue, Ruxton, facing St. John's AME Church

access: The tree stands on PRIVATE PROPERTY (owned by the Anastasiades family) but is directly beside and clearly visible from the public roadway (Bellona Avenue), which motorists and pedestrians pass under its canopy on every day. Visitors can view and photograph it from the road; there is no suggestion anyone may step onto the private lawn itself. State plainly: viewable from the road, not enterable.
transport: Ruxton, a suburb about 11km/7 miles north of downtown Baltimore; nearest Baltimore Light Rail stop is Falls Road, roughly 2km/a 25-minute walk away, otherwise a roughly 20-25 minute drive from downtown.
story:
Keeping this oak alive takes 5,000 gallons of water a week. The family who own the lawn it grows on pay for that, and for the fungicide treatments against the phytophthora working at its roots, because the tree leaning over Bellona Avenue was a seedling around 1646, twelve years after the first English colonists landed in Maryland.

By 1694 it was big enough to be useful. Surveyors used it to mark the boundary between two land grants, Young Man's Adventure and Samuel Hope, in the same year Maryland moved its government from St Mary's City to Annapolis. It outlasted the Bellona Gunpowder Works, which supplied ammunition for the War of 1812 nearby, and it was already close to two centuries old when the Baltimore and Susquehanna Railroad came through in the 1830s. Local legend has Abraham Lincoln catching sight of it from a train in 1863. Nobody has ever sourced that, and it is repeated here as legend rather than fact.

The Baltimore Sun measured it in 2002 at over 100 feet tall, with a canopy spanning roughly 150 feet and a trunk 18 feet around. A more recent account of the man who cares for it calls it nearly 400 years old and describes the watering still going on.

It grows on private ground. Stand on the road beneath the branches and look up, which is as far as anyone should go.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.49 metres round, under a canopy roughly 150 feet across that reaches out over the road. It stands at the corner of Dunlora Road and Bellona Avenue, facing St John's AME Church.
why_go: A white oak that was already generations old when Lincoln's train may have passed it in 1863, marking a property line drawn in 1694, still growing over Bellona Avenue on private land its owners keep alive with weekly deep watering.

name: The Frederick Douglass Elm

location.address: Intersection of West Hill Street and Sharp Street, Hermitage Park, Otterbein

verified_sources: search-corroborated citation of https://darkroom.baltimoresun.com/2017/06/baltimores-big-trees/ (page returned HTTP 500 on direct fetch this pass; its specific wording -- 'the orator addressed Baltimoreans beneath the same limbs, in 1878', location and species -- was corroborated identically across three independent search queries, but was not read on the page itself; treat as thin until a future pass can fetch it directly)
access: Free. Public property at a city street intersection in Otterbein, near Oriole Park at Camden Yards.
transport: Downtown Baltimore, Otterbein neighbourhood, walkable from Camden Yards and the Inner Harbor (about 10-15 minutes).
story:
Baltimore tradition holds that Frederick Douglass planted this elm as a boy, while he was still enslaved in the city. No document proves it. The people who pass the story on say some believe it, which is the honest form of the claim and the form we are keeping.

What is on the record is thinner and more solid: TreeBaltimore, the city's own forestry programme, lists this English elm among Baltimore's notable trees, standing where West Hill Street meets Sharp Street in Otterbein, a short walk from Camden Yards. By the same local memory, Douglass came back to it. An account repeated around the city, which we have not managed to read at its original source, says he addressed a Baltimore crowd beneath these limbs in 1878, forty years after he escaped slavery from this city and went north. Treat the return as story rather than record until somebody produces the page.

The species is its own piece of history. English elms went into American cities by the thousand in the nineteenth century, and Dutch elm disease took most of them from the 1930s onward, which is why a mature one on a street corner now stops people who know what they are looking at. Neighbours have reported bigger branches coming down in recent years.

Nobody has dated it and nobody has put a tape around it. If you know either number, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the elm on the corner, a species Dutch elm disease made rare on American streets. It stands where West Hill Street meets Sharp Street, at Hermitage Park in Otterbein, minutes from Camden Yards.
why_go: An English elm a Baltimore tradition says Frederick Douglass planted as an enslaved child, and where local memory holds he returned in 1878 to speak beneath its limbs as a free man; still standing minutes from Camden Yards.
